questions.q: A collision between two isolated objects occurs, but some kinetic energy becomes heat. Which statement can still remain true?
options: Total momentum is conserved even though kinetic energy is not.
Both momentum and kinetic energy must decrease.
Kinetic energy conservation requires momentum to change.
Heat production prevents conservation of momentum.
questions.why: Momentum is conserved in an isolated system; kinetic energy can be transformed into other forms.

questions.q: A planet's orbit becomes more elliptical after an interaction. At which part of the orbit is its speed greatest?
options: At its closest approach to the Sun
At its greatest distance from the Sun
At every point equally
Only when it crosses Earth's orbital plane
questions.why: An orbiting object moves faster when nearer the Sun, consistent with conservation of orbital energy and angular momentum.

questions.q: A spectrum from a star has absorption lines at the same pattern of wavelengths as a laboratory element but shifted together. What does the shared pattern indicate?
options: The element can be present in the star, while the shift can reveal relative motion.
The star must be made only of that element.
The element's lines are caused by the telescope's mirror shape.
The shift directly gives the star's distance without other information.
questions.why: Line patterns identify atoms or molecules, and a common shift can indicate Doppler motion.

questions.q: Two thermal sources have peaks at different wavelengths. Which source has the higher surface temperature?
options: The source whose spectrum peaks at the shorter wavelength
The source whose spectrum peaks at the longer wavelength
The source with the smaller apparent size, regardless of spectrum
Neither; peak wavelength contains no temperature information
questions.why: A hotter thermal source has its peak emission at a shorter wavelength.

questions.q: An atom emits a photon as an electron moves from a higher energy level to a lower one. Which statement must be true?
options: The photon carries energy equal to the difference between the levels.
The electron gains energy from the photon while moving downward.
The photon must be a radio wave regardless of the level spacing.
The atom's number of protons changes.
questions.why: The emitted photon carries the energy lost as the electron transitions between levels.

questions.q: A galaxy's spectral lines are shifted toward longer wavelengths. Which conclusion is best supported before other effects are considered?
options: The galaxy is receding along our line of sight.
The galaxy must be rotating so rapidly that it is breaking apart.
The galaxy is moving only across the sky with no radial motion.
The shift proves that its temperature is increasing.
questions.why: A redshift indicates motion away along the line of sight, though cosmological expansion can also contribute.

questions.q: A star's spectrum contains broad absorption features from both the star and Earth's atmosphere. What should an astronomer do to separate the sources?
options: Compare with reference or calibration observations of the atmosphere.
Assume every absorption feature came from the star.
Replace spectroscopy with a single colour image.
Use only the star's apparent position.
questions.why: The atmosphere can imprint absorption features, so calibration helps distinguish terrestrial from astronomical signals.

questions.q: A larger telescope produces a brighter image of a dim galaxy, but the galaxy's apparent size is unchanged. Which statement best explains this?
options: Aperture improves light collection; image scale and magnification are separate properties.
The aperture cannot affect recorded brightness.
The detector has become a gravitational-wave instrument.
The galaxy's physical size has changed.
questions.why: Aperture collects more light, while magnification and image scale address apparent size.

questions.q: An observatory combines two separated radio dishes and can distinguish a close pair of sources better than either dish alone. What has primarily improved?
options: Angular resolution from the longer effective baseline
The sum of the dish areas beyond their physical sizes
The atmosphere's transmission of X-rays
The intrinsic brightness of both sources
questions.why: Interferometry uses separation between telescopes to improve resolving power without enlarging each dish.

questions.q: A telescope's detector records a sharp image only when placed at one precise location behind the optics. What is that location?
options: The focal plane
The celestial equator
The horizon
The transmission window
questions.why: The focal plane is where incoming rays from a source are brought into focus.

questions.q: An orbit diagram shows Mercury, the asteroid belt, Jupiter, and a distant icy population in that order. Which interpretation best matches the solar-system structure?
options: Rocky inner planets precede the asteroid belt and outer giant planets, with icy bodies beyond.
The asteroid belt lies beyond the Oort cloud.
All icy bodies orbit inside Mercury's path.
The diagram proves the planets' sizes are drawn to scale.
questions.why: The broad order of the regions is inner rocky planets, asteroid belt, outer planets, and distant small-body populations.

img.alt: The Sun, inner planets, asteroid belt, outer planets, and distant icy bodies in orbital order.

questions.q: A world is similar to Earth in size but has a dense carbon-dioxide atmosphere and extreme surface heating. Which comparison is most useful?
options: Venus shows that similar size does not guarantee similar surface conditions.
Jupiter shows that rocky planets cannot retain atmospheres.
Mercury shows that every dense atmosphere causes extreme heating.
Neptune shows that all inner planets are ice giants.
questions.why: Venus and Earth are similar in size but have very different atmospheres and surface environments.

questions.q: A comet becomes active near the Sun and its tail points away from the Sun while the nucleus moves in another direction. Which process best accounts for this geometry?
options: Solar heating releases gas and dust that radiation and solar wind push outward.
The tail is a solid extension trailing the comet's velocity.
The comet's gravity bends its own tail toward the Sun.
The nucleus is pushed backward by Earth's atmosphere.
questions.why: Released gas and dust are pushed away from the Sun, so the tail direction is not simply behind the comet's motion.

questions.q: Which observation is the strongest evidence for a rotating disk during solar-system formation?
options: Most planets orbit in nearly the same plane and direction.
Every planet has the same number of moons.
All planets have exactly equal densities.
Every comet has a visible tail throughout its orbit.
questions.why: A flattened rotating disk naturally explains the coordinated orbital directions and planes.

img.alt: A collapsing cloud forms a rotating disk around a young Sun, where planetesimals accumulate.

questions.q: A small rocky body is round and orbits the Sun, but it shares its orbital neighborhood with many other sizable objects. Which classification is most appropriate?
options: Dwarf planet
Major planet
Natural satellite
Cometary coma
questions.why: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is nearly round but has not cleared its orbital neighborhood.

questions.q: A spacecraft must compare a surface mineral at one location with the composition of the planet as a whole. Which pairing provides the most complementary evidence?
options: A lander or rover for local analysis and an orbiter for broad mapping
Two flybys with no instruments
A light curve alone and a larger display screen
A terrestrial telescope and a clock
questions.why: Surface missions provide local measurements, while orbiters give repeated broad coverage.

questions.q: A space observatory detects radiation absorbed by Earth's atmosphere, while a ground telescope continues visible-light observations. Which conclusion follows?
options: Space and ground observatories provide complementary wavelength access.
Ground telescopes cannot collect any electromagnetic radiation.
The atmosphere blocks every wavelength equally.
The space observatory changes the source's emission.
questions.why: Ground instruments remain valuable in atmospheric windows, while space telescopes can access blocked wavelengths.
